Investing in a marketplace in Morocco: the complete guide

A marketplace in Morocco depends on the choice of niche, the trust of sellers and a journey adapted to local payment and delivery habits. This guide details those choices and explains how Codex runs this kind of product remotely.

In short

  • A precise niche and sellers recruited first are worth more than a broad, empty catalogue.
  • The interface is designed in Arabic and French, with payment through an approved gateway and, often, cash on delivery.
  • Legal and tax questions are confirmed with a local adviser before development.
  • Codex runs this kind of product remotely, with video workshops and a demo at each sprint.

In Morocco, many merchants, artisans and small brands already sell online, often through social media and messaging apps. A marketplace can bring them together on a single platform, with a searchable catalogue, tracked orders and common rules. Buyers gain choice and trust; the operator gains a model that usually earns a commission.

Making this kind of platform work takes precise choices: the niche, the languages, payment, delivery and the legal framework. This guide reviews them and explains how Codex works with project owners based in Morocco, entirely remotely.

01Choosing a niche and recruiting sellers first

A general marketplace launched without sellers stays empty. It is better to start with a segment where the offer is scattered and buyers struggle to compare, for example:

  • crafts and home decoration, which can also target customers abroad;
  • regional food products and fine groceries;
  • spare parts or professional equipment, where searching by reference saves time;
  • fashion and accessories from local designers.

These ideas need to be validated in the field. Once the niche is chosen, recruit sellers one by one, help them publish a careful catalogue, then invest in bringing in buyers.

02The essential features

  1. 01
    Seller space. Sign-up, document checks, and management of products, stock, prices and orders.
  2. 02
    Catalogue and search. Clear categories, useful filters and complete product pages in both languages.
  3. 03
    Multi-vendor cart. A single payment for the buyer, then split into sub-orders by seller.
  4. 04
    Commissions and payouts. Automatic commission calculation and tracking of what is owed to each seller.
  5. 05
    Reviews and disputes. Ratings reserved for buyers who received their order, and a return procedure arbitrated by the operator.
  6. 06
    Operator back office. Seller approval, listing moderation, order tracking and statistics.

The guide to creating a multi-vendor marketplace details each of these building blocks. For management, Codex has built tools such as AZ fulfillment, which brings orders, stock and statistics together in one dashboard.

03An interface in Arabic and French

Moroccan buyers often browse in Arabic as well as in French, and the interface must be designed for both from the start: right-to-left reading, text length, translated product pages. Darija, Moroccan Arabic, can have a place in marketing messages and on social media, depending on the audience; it is worth testing with your first customers. English can be added for a niche that targets export.

04Payments: an approved gateway and cash on delivery

Online card payment goes through an approved local payment gateway, with which the operator signs a contract. The platform does not store card data: it redirects the buyer and receives the confirmation.

Cash on delivery is often expected, especially for a first purchase on a platform that is still unknown. It reassures buyers but calls for precise tracking: collections per sub-order, refused parcels and payouts to sellers once the money comes back.

05Delivery and logistics partners

Delivery usually goes through specialised companies, chosen according to the cities covered and the quality of tracking. The points to plan:

  • who ships: each seller, or the operator from a central point;
  • fees by city and weight, shown before the order;
  • sending orders to the carrier and getting the tracking number;
  • handling returns and refused parcels.

06Legal and tax points to check

A marketplace creates obligations for the operator towards sellers and buyers alike. These topics are checked with a legal and tax adviser in Morocco, before development:

  • the entity that runs the platform and the status of the sellers admitted;
  • the terms of sale and terms of use;
  • the invoicing of commissions and the taxation of sales;
  • collecting payments for third parties and the protection of personal data.

07Working remotely with Codex

Codex has no office in Morocco. The team works remotely with project owners based in Morocco, using a method that makes follow-up as simple as meeting in person:

  • video workshops to scope the niche, the rules and the journeys;
  • shared mock-ups in Figma, commented on and approved screen by screen;
  • a demo of the platform at each sprint, on a test environment available online;
  • accounts, a domain and code in your name from the start.

To compare options, the article on development agencies in Morocco gives selection criteria.

08A useful first version, then improvements

The first version is usually a responsive website, easier to make known, with a seller space accessible from a browser. The Codex website development service covers this foundation. That first version contains:

  • a single niche, in Arabic and French;
  • the seller space and approval by the operator;
  • the multi-vendor cart, the payment gateway and cash on delivery;
  • the back office for orders, commissions and disputes.

Then, depending on real use: a mobile app, new categories, promotion tools for sellers or central logistics.

09Mistakes to avoid

  • opening several niches before one has succeeded;
  • translating the interface at the last minute instead of designing it in two languages;
  • ignoring cash on delivery and the handling of refused parcels;
  • launching before the legal and tax framework is confirmed with a local adviser;
  • publishing the platform on accounts that are not in your name.

10What changes the budget

The cost depends on the scope, not on a standard rate. The main factors:

  • the number of languages and niches at launch;
  • the integration with the payment gateway and delivery companies;
  • the commission and payout rules;
  • the level of moderation and dispute handling;
  • the target channels: website only, or website and mobile apps.

Codex sends a detailed quote after the scoping workshop. To prepare that meeting, read how to write a project brief.

11The steps with Codex

  1. 01
    Discovery. A video workshop on your niche, your sellers, payment and delivery. You leave with a clear scope, a schedule and a detailed quote.
  2. 02
    Design. The buyer and seller journeys in Arabic and French, the back office and the technical architecture. You approve every screen before development.
  3. 03
    Development. Short sprints with an online demo at each step, and tests on the multi-vendor cart, payment and returns.
  4. 04
    Launch and support. Go-live on a domain and accounts in your name, remote training for your team and the first sellers, then maintenance and new features.

FAQ

Your questions on this topic

Another question? Write to us, we reply quickly.

Does Codex have an office in Morocco?

No. Codex works remotely with project owners based in Morocco, with video workshops and a demo at each sprint.

Should you offer cash on delivery?

Often, yes, especially for first purchases. It comes in addition to online payment through an approved local gateway and calls for precise tracking of collections.

Should the interface be in Arabic and French?

Usually, yes. Both languages are designed from the start, including right-to-left display for Arabic.

What legal steps should you plan?

The operator’s entity, the status of sellers, the terms and conditions, taxation and data protection. These points are confirmed with a legal and tax adviser in Morocco.

How much does a marketplace in Morocco cost?

The price depends on the languages, the payment and delivery integrations, the commission rules and the target channels. Codex sends a detailed quote after the scoping workshop.

Can Codex build this marketplace?

Yes. Codex designs custom web platforms, apps and back offices in Arabic, French and English. The scope is set in a remote workshop, and the code stays in your name.
